UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


    Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company             )
                                                          )
    v.                                                    )
                                                                          Docket No. EL26-38-000
                                                          )
    Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.        )


                    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                          CONSUMERS ENERGY COMPANY

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Consumers Energy Company (“Consumers

Energy”) submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to address certain comments and

protests filed in response to the Complaint filed by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company

d/b/a CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (“SIGE”) on January 6, 2026 in this proceeding.2 In the

SIGE Complaint, SIGE requests that the Commission direct the Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) to revise its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve

Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to include a cost recovery schedule that SIGE has proposed for recovery

of costs associated with an emergency order issued by the U.S. Secretary of Energy (“Secretary”)

on December 23, 2025 (“DOE Order”) pursuant to Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 202(c) and

section 301(b) of the Department of Energy Organization Act.3




1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2025).
2
 Complaint Requesting Fast Track Processing, Docket No. EL26-38-000 (filed Jan. 5, 2026) (“SIGE
Complaint”).
3
    U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-13, at 2 (December 23, 2025).
           The DOE Order states the Secretary’s determination that an emergency exists within the

MISO region – specifically, in the northern and central zones of MISO – and directs SIGE to

ensure that Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley Generating Station (“Cully”), a coal-fired generating station

in Indiana, remains “available to operate” until March 23, 2026,4 notwithstanding plans to cease

operations on December 31, 2025.5 A number of parties that have intervened in this proceeding

have requested that the Commission require a MISO stakeholder process before the Commission

rules on the Complaint.6 But a MISO stakeholder process is unwarranted here, as the Commission

just recently found in rejecting similar arguments raised in response to a Complaint filed by

Consumers Energy.7 There is no reason for the Commission to depart from that recent finding,

and, for the reasons set forth in more detail below, the Commission should again reject requests to

direct MISO to commence a stakeholder process. Alternatively, should the Commission change

course and direct MISO to commence a stakeholder process, the Commission should clarify that

any such process would be forward looking only, and would not modify the already approved cost

recovery process in place for Consumers Energy’s J.H. Campbell Plant (discussed below) and any

existing or future DOE Orders to ensure continued availability of the Campbell Plant.

 I.        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          The Commission has discretion to accept answers to protests and regularly does so when

the information provided in the proposed answer will assist the Commission in its decision-making

process.8 Good cause exists for the Commission to accept this Answer because it corrects certain

misstatements in various comments filed in response to the SIGE Complaint, will “clarify the

issues in dispute,” will help the Commission “achieve a more complete and accurate record” in

this proceeding,9 and will assist the Commission in its decision-making process. Acceptance of

this Answer will not impede or delay Commission action.10 Consumers Energy respectfully

requests that the Commission accept this Answer and consider the points raised herein.

II.       ANSWER

          As the Commission is aware, in May 2025, the DOE issued an FPA section 202(c) order,

declaring a resource adequacy emergency in MISO zones 1 through 7 and directing the Company

to keep the J.H. Campbell Plant (“Campbell”) available to operate to address the emergency (“May

Campbell Order”).11 Consumers Energy immediately began complying with the May Campbell

Order. However, both the Company and MISO recognized that the MISO Tariff did not include a

Transmission, LLC, 190 FERC ¶ 61,110 at P 26 (2025) (“We accept Great Basin’s answer because it has

 NorAm Gas Transmission Co., 69 FERC ¶ 61,135 at 61,494 n.4 (1994); see also Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator
Corp., 105 FERC ¶ 61,284 at P 10 (2003) (granting motion for leave to file answer where the proposed
answer offered information clarifying the issues and would aid the Commission in its decision-making),
reh’g denied, 106 FERC ¶ 61,201 (2004).
10
  Dominion Transmission, Inc., 138 FERC ¶ 61,198, at P 5 n.3 (2012) (finding good cause to accept an
unauthorized answer where it “[did] not delay the proceeding, may assist the Commission in understanding
the issues raised, and will ensure a complete record.”) (citations omitted).
11
     U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-3 (May 23, 2025).


                                                     3
 mechanism for Consumers Energy to recover costs associated with complying with the May

Campbell Order, and MISO lacked authority to unilaterally offer the Company a section 202(c)

rate agreement. Accordingly, Consumers Energy filed a complaint and asked the Commission to

order MISO to adopt a new schedule that would allow Consumers Energy to recover costs

associated with the Campbell Order (and any future extensions), net of market revenue, and

provide for MISO to allocate such costs to load serving entities throughout MISO zones

1 through 7.12 The Commission ruled that the relief Consumers Energy requested was just and

reasonable and granted the Complaint.13 In doing so, the Commission expressly rejected calls for

the Commission to deny the Complaint and refer the matter to a MISO stakeholder process, among

other various arguments lodged by intervenors.14 The Commission reiterated in its Order on

Request for Rehearing that a stakeholder process related to the Proposed Tariff Provision was not

necessary.15 As explained in both the Complaint Order and the Rehearing Order, the Commission

found that states and other stakeholders were able to sufficiently participate in the proceeding

before FERC and that sufficient evidence was before the Commission to find Consumers’

proposed cost allocation methodology just and reasonable.16

           Since the May Campbell Order was issued, the DOE has issued two additional orders

requiring the continued availability of Campbell.17 And the DOE has issued similar orders to other

 generation owners, like SIGE. In response, SIGE has filed a complaint seeking relief that is

materially the same as the relief requested—and granted—in Consumers Energy’s complaint

proceeding.18 In response, a number of parties that intervened or protested in Consumers Energy’s

complaint proceeding (Docket No. EL25-90-000) have lodged similar arguments in response to

the SIGE Complaint.19

          In particular, a number of parties continue to call for the Commission to order MISO to

initiate a stakeholder process “to evaluate appropriate cost allocation and recovery approaches.”20

But, as explained in the Consumers Energy complaint proceeding docket, it would be inappropriate

for the Commission to seek to avoid resolving issues related to recovery of section 202(c) order

costs by directing a MISO stakeholder process.

          First, FPA section 202(c) contemplates that the Commission—not MISO—will address the

cost recovery issues arising from the DOE Order.21

          Second, calls for the Commission to direct a stakeholder process to resolve cost allocation

and evaluate who benefits from a given order are directly at odds with FPA section 202(c)’s

framework and allocation of responsibility. As with the 202(c) orders requiring Consumers

Energy to keep Campbell available, the Secretary determined in the 202(c) order directed at SIGE

and the Cully facility that keeping the facility available is necessary to address an emergency and




18
     Consumers Complaint Order.
19

similar complaint proceeding filed by Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO”) in
Docket No. EL26-36. As noted in its Answer filed in the NIPSCO proceeding, Consumers Energy urges the
Commission to again reject calls for a MISO stakeholder process and take a consistent approach across all
three dockets.

  OMS Comments at 4; see also MoPSC Comments; Illinois AG Comments at 3-6; ICC Comments at 3-
11.
21

                                                   5
 is in the public interest.      Cost allocation in all of these cases must track the Secretary’s

determinations, as stated in the relevant orders. The Commission so held in the Consumers Energy

complaint proceeding,22 and that ruling was correct. Moreover, both the DOE’s section 202(c)

orders, and the Commission’s orders determining the scope and nature of the emergency

conditions set forth in the DOE section 202(c) orders, are subject to challenge through the

opportunity for rehearing and judicial review. That opportunity for rehearing and judicial review

is the proper channel for challenging determinations regarding the scope and nature of the declared

emergency, and the conclusion that continued operation of a given generator is required to address

the emergency and, therefore, in the public interest. It would be inappropriate, and untenable, for

the Commission to order or initiate a process that might lead to different conclusions about whether

the continued availability of a given generator does or does not benefit ratepayers in the MISO

zones that the Secretary has declared are experiencing an emergency. Re-opening this issue would

introduce significant regulatory uncertainty for utilities and generation owners within MISO who

are subject to 202(c) Orders.

          Third, MISO has not called for a stakeholder process.23 Rather, as in the Consumers

Energy complaint proceeding, MISO has stated that it “supports the addition of a cost recovery

schedule to the Tariff” and “believes that a Commission finding that such a mechanism be

incorporated in the Tariff” would further compliance with the DOE Order.24 Consumers Energy

believes that, when a generation owner is compelled to keep operating a facility that was planned

     Consumers Complaint Order at P 39; Consumers Rehearing Order at P 32.
23
  To the extent that certain intervenors point to the approach that PJM Interconnection, Inc. (“PJM”) is
taking in response to a different 202(c) order, those comments are unavailing. PJM is a different

                                                     6
 to be retired, the Commission should ensure a timely and predictable process for that generation

owner to recover the costs associated with keeping the facility available (net of market revenue).

Accordingly, Consumers Energy submits that the Commission should reject arguments calling for

the implementation of a MISO stakeholder process.

          Finally, one commenter has argued that the uptick in the DOE’s issuance of 202(c)

orders—including orders requiring continued operation for additional 90-day periods (as with

Consumers Energy) as well as first-time orders to new generation owners (as with SIGE and the

Cully unit)—provides a basis for the Commission to now require a MISO stakeholder process,

even though the Commission declined to do so in the Consumers Energy proceeding.25 This

argument is unfounded and should be rejected. In fact, the uptick in 202(c) orders counsels in

favor of following an established process—not switching gears and creating regulatory uncertainty

by throwing issues into an ill-defined stakeholder process. Specifically, by granting Consumers

Energy’s Complaint, the Commission laid the groundwork for an orderly process when the DOE

directs a generator in MISO to remain available and not be retired: (1) a MISO generation owner

being required to defer retirement of a facility and keep it operational can request to have MISO

adopt a new Tariff schedule to permit allocation and recovery of 202(c) order costs; (2) such order

costs will be allocated according to the scope and nature of the emergency declared in the relevant

202(c) order, as determined by the Commission, and subject to judicial review; and (3) separate

from approval of a generator-specific schedule to be added to the MISO Tariff, actual costs to be

recovered for compliance with a 202(c) order will be presented in a 202(c) cost-recovery filing for

Commission approval. Beyond the certainty that this process provides, the Commission has




25
     Consumers Complaint Order at P 41.


                                                7
 already rejected the argument that the increased frequency of 202(c) referrals is reason to reject an

otherwise just and reasonable cost allocation proposal. 26

           The foregoing process, approved in the Consumers Energy complaint proceeding, is the

model that the Commission should continue to endorse for other 202(c) orders impacting

generation owners in MISO. To the extent that the Commission disagrees and adopts a different

approach going forward, the Commission should make clear that such a decision does not impact

its prior determination in the dockets related to Consumers Energy’s Campell Plant and the

continuing DOE orders requiring it to remain available, any and all of which orders should

continue to be covered by the cost recovery process approved by the Commission in Docket No.

Docket No. EL25-90-000.27

III.       CONCLUSION

           For the reasons discussed herein, Consumers Energy respectfully requests that the

Commission accept this Answer, reject requests to direct MISO to commence a stakeholder

process, and order MISO to adopt the cost recovery mechanism proposed by SIGE.
